# Why did the man put the white powder on it?

## Short answer

He powdered the upside-down steel bowl because of what he does next: he presses both flat
palms onto it for about twelve seconds and then lifts the bowl clean off the ground with
one **flat, open, un-gripping hand** — the bowl hangs in mid-air stuck to his bare palm.
The white powder is the preparation for that stunt. It is ordinary talcum-type body powder
(the shaker is labelled "Puder", German for powder), i.e. a dry, slippery,
moisture-absorbing dust. Sprinkling it over the bowl dries and de-tackifies the metal and
his skin, so the bowl's clinging to his open hand cannot be put down to glue, tape, sticky
or sweaty palms; at the same time it conditions the contact so his soft palm can seat
itself smoothly and evenly over the polished dome, and it keeps the bowl's rim from
sticking to the board underneath. In short: he put powder on it so that the bowl would
still cling to his flat bare hand from a dry, slippery, visibly un-sticky surface — the
powder both makes the demonstration work and proves that nothing adhesive is involved.

## What is on screen

* The scene is outdoors in bright sunshine, on a paved/gravel surface, in front of two
  large colourful abstract paintings leaning against a wall (the signature reads roughly
  "Megola"/"Mezala"). The man is older and bald, in a white dress shirt with the sleeves
  buttoned, a dark-red bow tie, black trousers and black dress shoes. He is clearly
  presenting/demonstrating something, not cooking.

  stainless-steel mixing bowls, all turned upside down, plus several pots and pans.

  talcum/baby-powder shaker, not a chemical reagent. There is extra handwritten marker
  text on the bottle that is too blurred to read.

1. **0–4 s** — static shot of the set-up.
2. **4–10 s** — he walks in, crouches down and deliberately holds both hands up to the

8. **35–39 s** — he stands up, rubs and dusts the powder off his fingers and hands, and

9. **39–46.7 s** — a static closing shot of the bowl standing on the board.

## Why the powder, stated point by point

1. **It is the set-up for a hand-adhesion demonstration.** The powder is applied
   immediately before the only real "event" in the clip: lifting a heavy steel bowl with a
   flat open palm and no grip. That is what the powder is for — everything about the
   sequence (clean palms shown first, powder second, long press third, lift fourth) is the
   order of a demonstration.
2. **It rules out glue, tape, sticky skin and sweat.** Talcum powder is the most
   anti-adhesive substance in an ordinary household: it is a dry mineral dust used
   precisely to stop things sticking and to soak up moisture. By showing his empty clean
   palms and then dusting both the bowl and his own fingers with it, he removes any
   suspicion that the bowl clings because his hand is damp, greasy, tacky or treated with
   something. This is the classic way such an effect is "proved" to an audience.
3. **It dries and conditions the contact between palm and polished steel.** A bare,

4. **It stops the bowl sticking to the board instead of to his hand.** He pushes powder

He put the white powder on the upside-down steel bowl (and on the board and his own

# Why he put the white powder on it

The white powder is dry talcum powder, baby powder, from the yellow shaker bottle that says “Powder” on it.

“It” is the small upturned stainless-steel bowl standing dome-up in the middle of the wooden board, and the board immediately around it.

The man shakes powder directly onto the dome of that bowl, tilts and turns the bowl to coat it, puts the bottle down, and rubs powder between his own palms. He then spends about fifteen seconds rubbing the dome vigorously with flat bare hands in small circles. This is a hand-rubbed singing-bowl demonstration: the rubbing is meant to drive the metal into strong resonant vibration. The copy of the video provided here has no audio track, so the ringing itself cannot be heard.

The reason for putting the powder on the bowl is to make that otherwise invisible vibration visible.

That is shown explicitly in the video. The loose grains bounce and are thrown off the metal as it resonates. The bowl starts coated white and ends clean and shiny, while the board around it becomes dusted white. When he lifts the bowl he reveals a circular cleared ring in the powder where the bowl sat. After he sets the bowl back down and takes his hands away, he flicks and sprinkles residual powder from his fingers above the still-ringing bowl, and a cloud of fine dust hangs and dances in the sunlight above the board. Without the powder the viewer would only see a man rubbing metal; with the powder the viewer sees the metal shaking the powder off, pushing it into a ring, and keeping fresh grains dancing in the air.

The powder has a practical enabling part of the same purpose. The dry talc absorbs sweat and skin oil from his palms and from the smooth steel, so his skin can get the controlled stick-slip grip needed to excite the resonance by friction instead of sliding silently. But the reason it is put on the bowl itself, in a visible white coat, is as a tracer: it turns sound and vibration into motion of white grains that the camera can see.
